home-energy-audit.title: Home energy audits in Halifax: EnerGuide evaluations, costs and rebates
home-energy-audit.description: Book an EnerGuide home energy audit in Halifax: booking through Efficiency Nova Scotia, local prices, Nova Scotia rebates and what 63% pre-1991 housing means for your upgrade list.
home-energy-audit.lede: In Nova Scotia, EnerGuide home evaluations are booked through Efficiency Nova Scotia's Home Energy Assessment program. Here's what one costs in Halifax, what it finds in Halifax's housing, and which rebates it unlocks.

sections.h2: What an evaluation finds in Halifax homes
sections.html:
Of Halifax's 121,700 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 63% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. The typical Halifax house dates from 1981–1990, and an evaluation is how you find out what that means for yours: the blower door measures air leakage, the advisor inspects the attic, walls, basement, windows and heating system, and the report ranks upgrades by what they'd save.

Halifax gets about 3,870 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −15.9°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Shearwater. That's right around the middle of the 70 cities we cover. The more heating a climate needs, the more each fix is worth, which is why the evaluation's ranked list matters more in some cities than others.

In the Halifax area, 26% of households heat mainly with a heat pump, 20% with electric baseboards, 20% with a boiler and radiators and 12% with a forced-air furnace; electricity is the main heating energy for 28% of households and oil for 23% (Statistics Canada, 2023). The heating system on the report shapes the recommendations: a forced-air furnace invites a ducted heat pump, electric baseboards a ductless one.
Efficiency Nova Scotia's Home Energy Assessment program charges a $199 program fee (waived for moderate-income households) and covers the initial and final assessments.

• Initial evaluation, about 2–3 hours. The advisor measures and inspects the house and runs the blower door test.
  • Report and EnerGuide rating. You get the home's energy rating in gigajoules per year and a list of recommended upgrades with estimated savings.
  • Do the work. Most rebate programs only count upgrades done after the initial evaluation.
  • Follow-up evaluation. A second visit measures the improvement, which is what most rebates pay on.

sections.h2: Why air leakage matters in Halifax
sections.html:
Halifax gets about 3,870 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −15.9°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Shearwater. That's right around the middle of the 70 cities we cover.

Of Halifax's 121,700 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 63% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older houses usually test leakier than newer ones, and an EnerGuide report compares your result with homes of the same era, so you can see whether your house is typical or a problem.

• Combustion safety. In the Halifax area, the main heating energy is oil for 23% of households. A tighter house changes how fuel-burning appliances vent, so the spillage check should be repeated after serious air sealing. Combustion safety testing in Halifax
  • Radon. Sealing shifts the pressure balance between the house and the soil. Health Canada's 2012 survey found 13.6% of 103 homes tested in the Zone 6 health region above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 38.7% (1 in 3) of houses at or above the guideline for the Halifax, NS (Halifax CMA) metro area. Test before and after big air-sealing jobs. Radon testing in Halifax

A blower door test is part of every EnerGuide evaluation rather than a separate purchase. Efficiency Nova Scotia's Home Energy Assessment program charges a $199 program fee (waived for moderate-income households) and covers the initial and final assessments.

• A calibrated fan is fitted into an exterior door and pulls air out until the house is at 50 pascals, the standard test pressure.
  • The result is air changes per hour at 50 Pa (ACH50): how many times an hour the whole volume of air would leak out and be replaced at that pressure.
  • While the fan runs, you and the advisor walk the house and feel for leaks at the attic hatch, rim joists, pot lights, trim and plumbing and wiring penetrations.
  • A second test after the work shows what changed, and it is what most rebates pay on.

heat-loss-calculation.title: Heat loss calculation in Halifax: sizing a heat pump for −15.9°C
heat-loss-calculation.description: A CSA F280 room-by-room heat loss calculation for Halifax homes, sized to the local −15.9°C design temperature: why it matters for heat pumps, what it costs and who does it.
heat-loss-calculation.lede: The heat loss calculation is how a heat pump or furnace gets sized for your house, and the key input is the design temperature: −15.9°C for Halifax, from NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Shearwater.

sections.h2: Why the design temperature matters in Halifax
sections.html:
−15.9°C is the 19th-mildest design temperature of the 70 cities we cover. The F280 calculation works out how much heat each room loses on that design day, from the house's actual walls, windows, air leakage and ceiling insulation.

At −15.9°C, a cold-climate heat pump sized to the calculation can carry most of the season, and the number shows how much backup heat the coldest days need.

In the Halifax area, 26% of households heat mainly with a heat pump, 20% with electric baseboards, 20% with a boiler and radiators and 12% with a forced-air furnace; electricity is the main heating energy for 28% of households and oil for 23% (Statistics Canada, 2023).

Contractors who size by square footage routinely oversize. An oversized heat pump costs more to buy, cycles on and off, dehumidifies poorly in summer and wears faster. An undersized one leans on backup heat. The F280 report is the evidence either way, and it's worth having before you compare quotes.

About $150–$400 as a standalone calculation (a September 2026 planning range; quotes vary). Many energy advisors bundle it with an EnerGuide evaluation, which also gives the calculation measured air-leakage data instead of an assumption.

ventilation-assessment.h1: Ventilation and humidity assessments in Halifax
ventilation-assessment.title: Ventilation and humidity assessment in Halifax: condensation, mold and HRVs
ventilation-assessment.description: Why Halifax homes get window condensation and musty air, what a ventilation and humidity assessment measures, and when an HRV or ERV makes sense. 22% of local houses were built since 2001.
ventilation-assessment.lede: Condensation on windows, musty basements and stuffy bedrooms are ventilation and humidity problems, and they're easy to confuse with insulation problems. A ventilation assessment measures which one you have.

sections.h2: Why Halifax homes get humidity problems
sections.html:
Halifax gets about 3,870 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −15.9°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Shearwater. On Halifax's coldest days, window glass and poorly insulated corners get cold enough for condensation at humidity levels that feel normal indoors, so winter humidity needs to stay at the lower end of the comfortable range.

Of Halifax's 121,700 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 63% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Newer houses (22% of Halifax's were built since 2001) are tight and usually have an HRV or ERV that needs balancing and cleaning. Older houses that get air-sealed can lose the accidental ventilation they used to rely on.

• Relative humidity in living areas and the basement.
  • Actual airflow from bath and kitchen fans, and whether they vent outside rather than into the attic.
  • How much fresh air the house gets, and whether an HRV or ERV is balanced.

sections.h2: What inspections find in Halifax attics
sections.html:
Of Halifax's 121,700 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 63% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Attics in older houses commonly have a fraction of today's recommended insulation, and top-ups done over the years often buried air leaks instead of sealing them first.

Halifax gets about 3,870 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −15.9°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Shearwater. That's right around the middle of the 70 cities we cover. The colder the climate, the faster added attic insulation pays for itself.

Vermiculite. Loose, pebbly, grey-brown or silver-gold insulation may contain asbestos. Health Canada's advice is not to disturb it; have it sampled before any attic work. Asbestos and vermiculite testing in Halifax

sections.h2: The right order for the work
sections.html:
• Seal the air leaks first: top plates, pot lights, plumbing stacks, the hatch.
  • Fix ventilation baffles so new insulation doesn't block soffit vents.
  • Then top up the insulation. Burying unsealed leaks under new insulation wastes much of the benefit.

radon-testing.title: Radon testing in Halifax: local levels, test kits and certified professionals
radon-testing.description: Radon in Halifax: Health Canada survey results for the Zone 6 region (13.6% above the guideline), how to test for 3+ months, where to get kits and C-NRPP professionals locally.
radon-testing.lede: Radon is invisible, has no smell, and is the second-leading cause of lung cancer in Canada. In Health Canada's national survey, 13.6% of homes tested in the Zone 6 health region were above the guideline, and the only way to know about your house is to test it.

glance.sub: the Halifax, NS (Halifax CMA) metro area

sections.html:
Health Canada's 2012 survey found 13.6% of 103 homes tested in the Zone 6 health region above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 38.7% (1 in 3) of houses at or above the guideline for the Halifax, NS (Halifax CMA) metro area.

The two surveys aren't directly comparable: the 2024 study pooled about 69,000 volunteer tests and more of them were taken in basements, which partly explains its higher numbers. Neither can tell you about a single house, because neighbouring homes can differ widely.

• Use a long-term test of at least three months, with most of it in the heating season, which gives the most conservative result.
  • Place the detector in the lowest level you spend four or more hours a day in, away from drafts, and follow the kit's instructions.
  • If the result is above 200 Bq/m³, Health Canada recommends fixing it within a year, sooner if it's much higher.

Our full radon testing guide.

• LungNSPEI's pilot Radon Reduction Grant Program provides free test kits and mitigation grants of up to $2,500 to low-income Nova Scotia households, and its library loan program lends detectors through public libraries; Nova Scotia also publishes a Radon Risk Map.
  • For a professional measurement or mitigation, search the C-NRPP directory by your Halifax postal code; it lists certified measurement and mitigation professionals.

sections.h2: Rules and help in Nova Scotia
sections.html:
• Nova Scotia's building code (the 2020 National Building Code, effective April 1, 2025) requires a radon rough-in in new homes.
  • The Canadian Lung Association's Lungs Matter program offers up to $1,500 toward mitigation for households with low to moderate incomes or a lung cancer diagnosis.
  • If your level is high, mitigation (usually a sub-slab depressurization fan system installed by a C-NRPP-certified professional) typically costs $2,000–$4,000.

faq.q: Is radon a problem in Halifax?
faq.a: Health Canada's 2012 survey found 13.6% of 103 homes tested in the Zone 6 health region above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 38.7% (1 in 3) of houses at or above the guideline for the Halifax, NS (Halifax CMA) metro area. Any home can have high radon, so Health Canada recommends testing every home.

faq.q: How long should a radon test take?
faq.a: At least three months, with most of it during the heating season. Short tests can't tell you your long-term average.

faq.q: Where can I get a radon test kit in Halifax?
faq.a: LungNSPEI's pilot Radon Reduction Grant Program provides free test kits and mitigation grants of up to $2,500 to low-income Nova Scotia households, and its library loan program lends detectors through public libraries; Nova Scotia also publishes a Radon Risk Map. Hardware stores and lung associations also sell long-term kits for about $30–$60.

faq.q: What does radon mitigation cost?
faq.a: Typically $2,000–$4,000 for a sub-slab depressurization system installed by a C-NRPP-certified professional.

mold-testing.title: Mold testing in Halifax: air quality sampling and finding the moisture source
mold-testing.description: Mold and indoor air quality testing in Halifax: when sampling is worth $300–$600, why damp coastal winters cause condensation, and how to find an accredited lab.
mold-testing.lede: Mold sampling tells you whether there's a hidden mold problem and roughly where. It doesn't tell you why, and fixing the moisture source is the actual cure.

sections.h2: Why mold shows up in Halifax homes
sections.html:
Halifax gets about 3,870 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −15.9°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Shearwater. Mild, wet winters keep materials damp, so poorly vented bathrooms, basements and crawlspaces are the usual suspects.

Of Halifax's 121,700 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 63% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older basements without a moisture barrier and houses that were air-sealed without adding ventilation are common trouble spots.

• You smell mustiness but can't find the source.
  • After a leak or flood, to check that cleanup worked.
  • Before buying an older house with signs of past water damage.

If you can see mould, you usually don't need a test to know it's there; you need to fix the moisture and clean it up properly.

No Canadian province has a mandatory mould standard for homes. Health Canada's guideline sets no numerical limit: it says to fix moisture problems and clean up visible mould.

Ask any Halifax tester which lab analyzes their samples, and look for one accredited under AIHA's EMLAP program for environmental microbiology. Pair sampling with a ventilation and humidity assessment, which finds the cause.

Ventilation and humidity assessments in Halifax · Our mold and indoor air quality guide

faq.q: How much does mold testing cost in Halifax?
faq.a: Plan on about $300–$600 for a typical sampling visit (a September 2026 planning range); lab fees for extra samples add to that.

faq.q: Do I need a test if I can see mould?
faq.a: Usually not. Visible mould needs cleanup and a fix for the moisture source. Testing helps most when you suspect mould you can't see.

faq.q: Is there a legal mould limit for homes in Canada?
faq.a: No. Health Canada sets no numerical limit; its guidance is to control moisture and clean up mould. Quebec has a voluntary handling standard.

lead-paint-testing.description: 22% of Halifax's houses were built before 1961, when lead paint was common. How to test with $15–$40 swabs or a lab, and how to renovate safely.

sections.h2: Which Halifax homes are at risk
sections.html:
Of Halifax's 121,700 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 63% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

  • Built before 1960: probably has lead-based paint (Health Canada).
  • Built 1960–1990: exterior paint may contain lead, and interior paint may contain smaller amounts.
  • Built after 1990: consumer paints were virtually lead-free by then.

• Swab kits ($15–$40) give a quick screen of the surfaces you plan to disturb.
  • For certainty, send paint chips to a lab accredited under AIHA's ELLAP program, or hire a firm with an X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analyzer.
  • Test before sanding, stripping or replacing old windows and trim.

Our lead paint guide.

Don't dry-sand, use a heat gun or power-wash it. Contain the work area, mist surfaces, clean with a HEPA vacuum, and keep children and pregnant people away until cleanup is done. No province has a lead-paint rule aimed at homeowners, but contractors in B.C. and Yukon must include lead in pre-renovation or demolition hazard inspections.

faq.q: Does my Halifax house have lead paint?
faq.a: If it was built before 1960, probably; 1960–1990, possibly on the exterior. Test the surfaces you plan to disturb.

faq.q: Are lead test swabs reliable?
faq.a: They are a useful screen. For renovation decisions, confirm with a lab analysis of paint chips or an XRF reading.

faq.q: What does lead paint testing cost?
faq.a: Swab kits run about $15–$40; lab analysis and XRF testing cost more and are quoted by the firm.

commercial-energy-audit.title: Commercial energy audits in Halifax: reporting rules and incentives
commercial-energy-audit.description: Commercial and multi-unit building energy audits in Halifax: ASHRAE levels, no mandatory reporting rule, and 3 utility or government incentives for audits and studies.
commercial-energy-audit.lede: Offices, apartment buildings, retail and industrial sites get engineering energy audits rather than EnerGuide evaluations. Here's what applies in Halifax: no mandatory reporting rule and 3 incentive programs we found for audits and studies.

sections.h2: Reporting rules that apply in Halifax
sections.html: • No city-specific rule found (none found): No municipal energy/water benchmarking, reporting or building-performance by-law found; provincial rules apply (see rules.provinces.NS).

• Free energy assessments for small businesses (Small Business Energy Solutions) (Efficiency Nova Scotia): Free energy assessment (in person or by phone) with a custom report on the best upgrades and available rebates. Details
  • Building Energy Retrofits (Custom Retrofit) - scoping and feasibility study incentives (Efficiency Nova Scotia): Scoping study rebate: 50% of cost up to $1,000 (P.Eng-signed). Feasibility study incentive: up to $15,000 (up to 100% of study cost) with pre-approval, paid at 100% if the project goes ahead to a Custom Project Agreement and 50% if it doesn't. Implementation incentive: the larger of $0.15/kWh or $250/kW of peak demand savings, limited to 50% of incremental costs and $750,000 per project, minus any study incentives. Details
  • Building Optimization Program (recommissioning) (Efficiency Nova Scotia): Funding covers 100% of an Investigation Study, up to $5,000, to assess building systems and recommend operational (recommissioning) improvements. Details

• Level 1, walk-through: a site visit and bill review that benchmarks the building and lists low-cost measures.
  • Level 2, energy survey and analysis: where the energy goes, with savings and cost estimates per measure. Most incentive applications use this level.
  • Level 3, detailed analysis: monitoring and modelling for capital-intensive projects.

Ask which level a quote covers. Audits are done by engineering firms and energy consultants; look for a P.Eng. and credentials such as the Certified Energy Manager (CEM). How commercial energy audits work.

faq.q: Do Halifax buildings have to report energy use?

faq.q: Are there incentives for commercial energy audits in Halifax?

Check eligibility and pre-approval rules before you commission the audit.
